newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Gulf War troops said not told about drug.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Gulf War troops said not told about drug.

text.p: The Pentagon said on Thursday it did not tell U.S. troops in the 1991 Gulf War that an anti-nerve gas drug they took was experimental because it did not want Iraq to learn of U.S. defences.

"I believe there was a conscious decision made at the time not to tell the troops," a spokesman, Captain Michael Doubleday said. "And the reason that that was done was that there was enormous concern at the time of raising any specter and any concern ... with the Iraqis that we were prepared to defend against certain kinds of chemical weapons."

The drug was pyridostogmine bromide and investigators are studying whether its use in combination with insecticides or other chemicals U.S. troops were exposed to might be a cause for illnesses veterans have suffered since the war.
"In retrospect had circumstances been otherwise we probably would have proceded differently," Doubleday said.
But he said the Defence Department believed then and believes now that the drug is safe and would have been an effective defence if Iraq had launched nerve gas against coalition forces.
He said a large study found that fewer than one-tenth of one percent of the troops suffered side effects such as nausea and cramps that would have caused them to be taken off the drug.
